clue.text: Dora sleeps rough she is spotted in the jungle

definitions.text: she is spotted in the jungle

indicators.note: rough treatment knocks the letters of the two words before it out of their order

explanation.surface: A girl called Dora beds down outdoors while someone in the jungle catches sight of her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rough' signals rearranging the ten letters of DORA SLEEPS. 'spotted' looks like 'seen' but describes the big cat's coat.
explanation.definitionFit: A female leopard is a jungle cat with a spotted coat, so she is literally spotted.

clue.text: All there, detectives follow central clue

indicators.note: follow says the detectives come after the other piece
central means the middle letters of clue are taken

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, British police detectives

explanation.surface: Police officers pursue the vital piece of evidence, everyone present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detectives follow' puts the police squad after the piece 'central' takes from 'clue'. 'All there' means mentally sound, not everyone present.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is all there is sane and clear-headed, thinking clearly.

clue.text: Rifle-ammo improved to the French standard

indicators.note: improved says the letters are reworked into something new

explanation.surface: Better rifle ammunition was brought up to the level of the French army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'improved' rearranges RIFLE-AMMO. 'standard' looks like a level of quality; it is a banner.
explanation.definitionFit: The oriflamme was the red banner of the abbey of Saint-Denis, carried as the battle flag of medieval French kings.

clue.text: Sue, for example, called name in acid-rain circles

indicators.note: circles means goes round and round, so the letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman called Sue gives her name among campaigners against acid rain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sue, for example, called' is a definition by sound: said aloud, 'Sue' is Sioux, a Plains people. 'circles' rearranges NAME IN ACID-RAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sioux are a Native people of the North American plains, a nation of the continent's first inhabitants.

clue.text: Spiny fish short of oxygen force throws it out

indicators.note: short of means lacking, so the element is removed from the fish

parts.note: a dragonet is a small, often brightly coloured spiny-finned fish
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A prickly fish starved of air is ejected by sheer force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'force' reads as physical strength; it is the police force, who throw out a dragnet to catch suspects.
explanation.definitionFit: A dragnet is a net dragged along to trap fish, and by extension a wide police search the force casts.

clue.text: County, losing tail, joins a league -—how bizarre

indicators.note: losing tail means the last letter of the county is dropped

parts.note: Surrey is a county south of London

explanation.surface: A county cricket side, without its final batsman, enters a league: strange.
explanation.walkthrough: SURREY is a county in south-east England; 'losing tail' drops its last letter. 'how bizarre' is an exclamation that something is dreamlike.
explanation.definitionFit: Surreal describes something weirdly dreamlike, so the exclamation means 'how dreamlike and strange'.

clue.text: Home fixture for City

explanation.surface: A football match played at home on behalf of a club called City.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home fixture' reads as a sports match; here it is a plumbed-in tub in a house. BATH is also a city in Somerset, in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A tub for washing is fitted permanently in a house, and the Roman spa town in Somerset bears the same name.

clue.text: With full expenses completely exhausted

explanation.surface: With every cost covered, someone is utterly worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: An all-in price includes every charge; all in also means worn out.
explanation.definitionFit: An inclusive price covers every charge, and someone tired to the point of collapse is worn out.

clue.text: Wild blows shake army installation

indicators.note: an installation sets things up in a new arrangement, so the letters are set out afresh

explanation.surface: Violent gusts rattle a military base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'installation' reads as a military base; it signals setting the letters of SHAKE ARMY up afresh. 'blows' looks like gusts of wind but means punches.
explanation.definitionFit: A haymaker is a wild, swinging punch thrown with all one's weight.

clue.text: One half can be written as one in this formal piece

definitions.text: One half can be written as one in this

parts.note: proper means correct and formal in manner
a fraction is a small part or piece

explanation.surface: A stiffly written piece of prose in which half of something can be set down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'formal piece' reads as a stiff essay; the pieces are PROPER and FRACTION. One half (1/2) is a fraction whose top number is below its bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: A fraction with a smaller numerator than denominator, value under one, such as a half, is called proper.

clue.text: Wild idea to enter him in medley-race

indicators.note: to enter says one piece goes inside another, here the pronoun going into the jumbled race
a medley is a mixture, so the letters of race are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone proposes signing a man up for the mixed-stroke swimming relay, an unlikely notion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'medley' turns the race into CERA, and 'to enter' places the pronoun after its first letter. A medley race is a real swimming event, which hides the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimera is a fanciful, impossible notion, a figment of the imagination.

clue.text: Game marshal concerned with the country

parts.note: RU stands for rugby union, a ball game
to marshal troops is to rally them, gather them together

explanation.surface: An official steward at a sporting event takes an interest in national affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'marshal' looks like a noun, a steward at the game, but works as the verb 'gather'. 'the country' here means the countryside, not a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Done in a rustic way, in relation to farmland and villages rather than towns.

clue.text: Playing dead by agreement

parts.note: D is a standard abbreviation for dead, as in genealogies
an alliance is a pact or agreement between parties

explanation.surface: Pretending to be a corpse by mutual arrangement, as children do in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing dead' reads as a single phrase; the definition is 'Playing' alone, in the sense of toying or trifling.
explanation.definitionFit: Dalliance is idle toying or flirtation, the act of playing around with someone or something.

clue.text: Leaflet from place near Harrow, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly says we want a word that is said like the name of the place

parts.note: Pinner is a suburb of north-west London beside Harrow

explanation.surface: A handbill handed out in a town near Harrow, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaflet' suggests a printed handout, but in botany it is one segment of a compound leaf. PINNER is a London suburb next to Harrow; in a non-rhotic British accent it sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany a pinna is one of the separate small leaves along the stalk of a compound leaf such as a fern frond.

clue.text: Short stop for a butterfly

explanation.surface: A brief halt made on account of a butterfly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short stop' suggests a pause on a journey; it is the punctuation mark that marks a short pause, shorter than a full stop. The comma is also a British butterfly with a comma-shaped white mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The punctuation mark makes a brief pause in a sentence, and an orange woodland butterfly is named after the white mark on its wing.

clue.text: Tropic island grain

parts.note: Capri is an Italian island in the Bay of Naples
corn is grain

explanation.surface: A tropical island known for its cereal crop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tropic' looks like an adjective for the island; it is one of the two tropics, the line of latitude south of the equator.
explanation.definitionFit: The southern line of latitude at about 23 degrees south is named after the goat of the zodiac.

clue.text: Play patience?

explanation.surface: Is a card game of patience something to play?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' and 'patience' both suggest games; play is the slack allowed in a machine part, and patience is forbearance.
explanation.definitionFit: Engineers call the permitted slack or variation in a part its allowance, and putting up with others is forbearance.

clue.text: Mostly pleasant, a students' prank at university, taking on a country

indicators.note: taking on says the last piece is added to the end
mostly means most but not all of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: nice means pleasant
a rag is a British student stunt, often for charity during rag week
U is an abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A fairly cheerful student stunt at college takes on a whole nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' trims NICE to NIC. A rag is a student prank, from the British university custom of rag week, held to raise money for charity.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicaragua is a republic in Central America.

clue.text: Cliff's epic price revision

definitions.note: Cliff's stands for 'Cliff is', with the 's as the verb

indicators.note: a revision reworks something, so the letters of the two words are reordered

explanation.surface: Someone called Cliff has rewritten the amount charged for a long poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revision' rearranges EPIC PRICE. 'Cliff' looks like a man's name; it is the steep rock face.
explanation.definitionFit: A precipice is a very steep rock face, a sheer drop.

clue.text: Pagan in unfinished Fielding novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the remaining letters are put in a fresh order
unfinished means the last letter of the name is left off

explanation.surface: A heathen appears in an incomplete novel by Henry Fielding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book by Fielding; it is the anagram signal for FIELDIN, which 'unfinished' leaves from FIELDING.
explanation.definitionFit: An infidel is an unbeliever, someone outside the faith, as a heathen is.

clue.text: Utter demand to support former partner

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece that supports another sits below it

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse or partner
a claim is a demand for something owed

explanation.surface: Making a demand to help pay for an ex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support' looks like maintenance paid to an ex; in a down clue it means the demand is written beneath the partner. 'Utter' is the verb 'say', not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To exclaim is to cry out or say something suddenly, to speak out.

clue.text: Contests of rare champions

parts.note: aces are experts or champions at something

explanation.surface: Tournaments made up of unusual winners.
explanation.definitionFit: Races are competitions of speed, contests to finish first.

clue.text: Piece of Virgil I adapted for Greek epic

indicators.note: Piece of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A section of the Roman poet's work that I reworked to serve as a Greek epic.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition included 'for', but 'for' only links wordplay to definition; 'Greek epic' alone defines. Virgil wrote the Aeneid, a Latin epic, which tempts the solver towards Roman works.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's long poem about the siege of Troy is the best-known epic of ancient Greece.

clue.text: Finger most often crossed in libraries?

explanation.surface: Which finger is most often crossed for luck inside libraries?
explanation.walkthrough: Crossed fingers suggest luck; the second sense is the library catalogue that readers go through to find books.
explanation.definitionFit: The forefinger beside the thumb has the same name as the alphabetical list in a library that readers search through.

clue.text: Dignity shown by eccentric people in US honours

parts.note: face is dignity or standing, as in losing face
cards are amusing or eccentric characters

explanation.surface: Respectability is on display from oddballs receiving American awards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'honours' suggests awards; in card games the honours are the top cards. In American usage the jack, queen and king are face cards (British court cards).
explanation.definitionFit: Kings, queens and jacks, picture cards ranking among the high honours in a pack, are called face cards in America.

clue.text: Top player, at end of July, is off-colour

parts.note: a seed is a ranked top player in a tennis tournament

indicators.note: at end of means the final letter of July is taken

explanation.surface: A leading tennis player, at the end of July, feels unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Wimbledon ends in July, which supports the tennis picture. 'off-colour' means unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Seedy means slightly unwell, run-down.

clue.text: Ancient Mariner, experienced performer

parts.note: ancient means old
a hand is a sailor, a member of a ship's crew

explanation.surface: Coleridge's Ancient Mariner is described as a seasoned actor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ancient Mariner' reads as Coleridge's poem; it splits into two pieces. 'experienced performer' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A veteran with long practice at something is called a skilled veteran or old-timer.

clue.text: Glowing all over at fireside

parts.note: an ingle is a fireplace or hearth, as in inglenook

explanation.surface: Someone is warm all over sitting by the hearth.
explanation.walkthrough: AT is taken as written. INGLE, a fireside, survives mainly in 'inglenook', a corner beside an open fire.
explanation.definitionFit: Tingling all over with excitement or warmth, the skin glowing and prickling.

clue.text: Neighbouring in kitchen extension

indicators.note: in says the answer sits within the words that follow, across the gap between them

explanation.surface: An extra room built on beside the kitchen is next door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points inside 'kitchen extension', where the letters run across the join of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Next means adjacent, the one beside or nearest.

clue.text: Simple to place lead against ray-damage

indicators.note: against means placed up beside, so the second piece goes next to the first

parts.note: lead is a chemical element, Pb

indicators.note: damage signals that the letters of ray are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: It is easy to put lead shielding up to protect against harm from radiation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead' looks like the shielding metal; it gives ELEMENT, since lead is one. 'damage' turns RAY into ARY, set 'against' ELEMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Elementary means basic and easy, at the most rudimentary level.
